channel.title: The Dig — Fault-tolerant architecture
channel.description: Codes, decoders and layouts — what a logical qubit costs, end to end. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the Fault-tolerant architecture preset. 5 pay dirt · 3 worth a look.

item.title: Improved Transversal Non-Clifford Gates from Cup Products
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Length-n quantum LDPC codes achieve distance d≥n(1−ϵ)/r with constant stabilizer weight and support depth-1 transversal non-Clifford Cr−1Z gates on logical yield s≥n1−ϵ disjoint tuples for any constant r≥3 and ϵ>0. Yield-distance product surpasses ds≫n, reaching magic state overhead exponent γ=log⁡(n/s)/log⁡(d)→0.

Grade 0.542 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Louis Golowich, Itzhak Tamo, Guanyu Zhu

Asks

Can quantum codes with constant-weight stabilizers support transversal non-Clifford gates that achieve distance and logical yield with ds≫n?

Before

All prior constant-stabilizer-weight qLDPC codes supporting constant-depth transversal CCZ had ds≤O(n), requiring limn→∞⁡γ≥1 (Zhu 2025, Lin-Li-Le 2026); beating this tradeoff previously required poly⁡log⁡(n) stabilizer weight (Golowich-Lin 2025).

But

Asymptotic regime n→∞ with constant gate order r≥3 and arbitrary constant ϵ>0. Linear yield s=Ω(n) requires stabilizer weight and circuit depth nϵ.

Tools

cup products · cochain complexes · classical Tanner codes · punctured tensor products · algebraic geometry codes

Abstract

It is a major challenge in quantum fault-tolerance to obtain low-overhead protocols for performing non-Clifford gates. In this vein, we construct quantum codes with low-weight stabilizers that support transversal (i.e. low-depth) implementations of the non-Clifford C^(r-1)Z gate, for every constant r≥3. In particular, we obtain length-n quantum LDPC codes (with constant-weight stabilizers) of polynomial distance d≥n^((1-ε)/r) supporting transversal C^(r-1)Z gates on a close-to-linear number k≥n^(1-ε) of disjoint tuples of logical qubits, for arbitrarily small ε>0. Our construction is the first with constant-weight stabilizers that obtains dk≫n, and as a consequence achieves arbitrarily small magic state overhead exponent γ=log(n/k)/log(d)>0. Comparable prior constructions instead required at least polylogarithmic stabilizer weight. We also show how to obtain linearly many k=Ω(n) logical C^(r-1)Z gates, though with stabilizer weight and physical circuit depth n^ε. We show that our transversal gates also support addressing (i.e. targeting) of specific logical qubits. To obtain our codes, we develop a general transformation based on cup products that maps classical codes satisfying a multiplication property to quantum codes with transversal C^(r-1)Z. We apply this transformation to a new family of classical Tanner codes that we construct from punctured tensor products of algebraic codes.

item.title: Purely-logarithmic-time- and constant-space-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Fault-tolerant quantum computation achieves constant space overhead with strictly logarithmic physical time overhead of depth O(Dlog⁡(WD/ε)) using $O(W + F(n))$ physical qubits for adaptive Clifford+CCZ circuits.

Grade 0.518 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Zhengyi Han, Zi-Wen Liu

Asks

Can constant-space-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation achieve strictly logarithmic time overhead?

Before

was O(log1+o(1)⁡(|C|/ε)) time overhead with constant space overhead (Nguyen and Pattison 2024)

But

Holds below a constant physical error threshold under locally stochastic noise, with ideal all-to-all physical qubit connectivity, noiseless classical processing, and sufficiently large width W≥CFF(n).

Tools

good quantum locally testable codes (qLTCs) · polynomial-subrank transversal logical CCZ gates · single-shot decoding · Hamming purification of Y states · recursive quantum Reed-Solomon magic-state distillation

Abstract

We prove that constant-space-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation can be achieved with provably strictly logarithmic time overhead, improving over the best known results with additional subpolylogarithmic factors. Our main construction uses polynomial-subrank transversal logical CCZ gates on good quantum locally testable codes to implement addressable universal computation by transferring batches of logical qubits between dense storage and active logical subspaces while reusing the same ancillary workspace. Logical CCZ gates are implemented directly by the transversal operation, so only stabilizer resource states require separate preparation. Furthermore, we give an alternative construction that also achieves purely logarithmic time overhead based on modifying the quantum Reed--Solomon magic-state distillation scheme of Nguyen and Pattison. Recursively applying a fixed distillation circuit protected by qLTCs of increasing block length eliminates the subpolylogarithmic time factor.

item.title: Soft decoding for quantum LDPC codes with experimental validation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Soft beam search decoding based on cumulative belief-propagation iteration cutoff yields up to 580× logical error suppression at physical error rate 10−3 with 0.1% rejection in simulations, and more than doubles fitted logical qubit lifetimes on trapped-ion experimental data with 2.6%–5.6% rejection per round.

Grade 0.482 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold” · Arda Aydin, Edwin Tham, Nicolas Delfosse, Min Ye

Figure

Logical bit error rate plotted against restart rate for sliding-window decoding of 4-round error-detected measurements in Q54 and Q70 codes at physical error rate 10−3. Tuning the iteration cutoff reduces error rate by up to 210× with 0.5 percentage points added restart rate.

Asks

Can soft decoding confidence metrics be extracted directly from quantum LDPC beam search decoder execution without additional decoder invocations or likelihood calculations?

Before

Two-round logical-error criterion (2R-LEC) required multiple decoding passes and 1.5–3.1× higher mean belief propagation iteration counts; hard decoding on trapped-ion data achieved breakeven lifetime near physical qubit baseline of 3.84±0.48 s (Tham 2026).

But

Simulations assume circuit-level noise at physical rates p=10−3 and p=3×10−3; experimental validation performed via post-selection re-analysis of existing 1-to-6 syndrome cycle datasets.

Tools

belief-propagation beam search decoder · iteration-cutoff post-selection · sliding-window streaming decoder · circuit-level noise simulations · trapped-ion experimental qLDPC dataset

Abstract

The decoder is a critical component of a fault-tolerant quantum computer, computing corrections based on parity-check measurements performed throughout the computation. A soft decoder supplements its output with a confidence score which, when used alongside post-selection, can substantially improve logical performance. We introduce a soft beam search decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that uses internal decoder data as a confidence metric, removing the need for extra computation. We perform circuit-level simulations of five quantum LDPC codes relevant for superconducting and trapped ion architectures equipped with our global soft decoder and we obtain up to 580× logical-error suppression at a physical error rate of 10⁻³ while rejecting only 0.1% of shots. Then, we simulate an error detected measurement, which is a core logical operation of the walking cat architecture, using a streaming version of soft beam decoder and we achieve up to 210× error suppression while increasing the rejection probability by only 0.5 percentage points. Finally, we revisit recent quantum LDPC code memory experiments on trapped ions, demonstrating that our soft decoder doubles the logical qubit lifetimes at the price of a mean rejection rate of 2.6%--5.6% per syndrome round, bringing all five codes into the beyond-breakeven regime.

item.title: Near-optimal high-rate surgery from linear PCPPs
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Constructs a sparse high-rate surgery gadget of size μ1+o(1) in polynomial time in μ to measure all t≤k logical qubits in a subcode of size μ≤n of an arbitrary $[[ n, k, d ]]$ quantum LDPC CSS code, with phenomenological fault distance ≥d across d rounds.

Grade 0.442 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Alexander Cowtan, Benjamin Ide

Asks

How to design quantum LDPC surgery gadgets that measure large sets of logical operators in parallel while preserving code sparsity, maintaining fault distance, and minimizing auxiliary space overhead?

Before

Thickening required 𝒪(μd) ancillary space and 𝒪(n3) spacetime volume for good codes with t=Ω(k) (Cowtan et al. 2024), while parallel branching required 𝒪~(t𝔴) space and 𝒪~(n3) spacetime volume (Cohen et al. 2024).

But

Constants are unoptimized and practicality at finite blocklengths is untested; spacetime detectors are dense rather than sparse; measurement applies to predetermined subcodes rather than full arbitrary Pauli product addressability.

Tools

linear Probabilistically Checkable Proofs of Proximity (PCPPs) · cochain complexes with relative cosystolic expansion · weight reduction via expander graphs · restriction of scalars

Abstract

A central problem for surgery with quantum Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes is the design of auxiliary systems which measure large sets of logical operators in parallel, while preserving sparsity and fault distance. We introduce a very general method for designing surgery gadgets which are 'high rate', meaning that the number of operators measured in parallel is large in comparison to the size of the auxiliary system. Given an arbitrary initial $[[ n, k, d ]]$ quantum LDPC Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code, and an arbitrary subcode of size μ≤n that contains t ≤k logical qubits, the method produces a sparse high-rate surgery gadget with size μ(logμ)^(O(loglogμ))=μ^(1+o(1)) which measures all t logicals in the subcode. The space overhead is asymptotically optimal up to subpolynomial factors, as the lower bound is Ω(μ). This gadget is produced in time polynomial in μ. When logical measurement is performed using these surgery gadgets, the phenomenological fault distance is at least d when performed for d rounds. Our main result comes from relating surgery gadgets with relative cosystolic expansion to linear Probabilistically Checkable Proofs of Proximity (PCPPs), which allow a randomised verifier to probabilistically verify the input to a linear circuit, using only oracle access to the input and a claimed proof.

item.title: Decoder-Prior Poisoning in Quantum Error Correction: Attacks and PriorGuard Defense
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Poisoning 6.4% (k=100) of high-influence decoder-prior entries increases logical error rate by 3.35× without modifying syndrome streams. PriorGuard rejects evidence-inconsistent updates and restores near-clean error rates with 1.7 to 1.8 ms latency and under 0.31 MB auxiliary memory per update.

Grade 0.442 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Xinyi Li, Yifeng Peng, Juntao Chen, Ying Wang

Figure

Logical error rate ratio and recovery ratio across different attack configurations, comparing PriorGuard with baselines including signed authentication, global clipping, and random monitoring.

Asks

Can adversarial manipulation of the classical calibration-to-decoder prior-update path alter quantum error correction decisions, and can such attacks be defended against without modifying syndrome streams?

But

Evaluated on rotated surface-code memory circuits with distances d∈{5,7,9}, d syndrome rounds, and base circuit-level noise probability 0.0045; does not address adaptive diffuse poisoning.

Tools

PriorGuard update gate · Stim rotated surface-code simulations · PyMatching decoder · Detector error model (DEM) single-edge ablation

Abstract

Quantum error correction (QEC) protects quantum computations by repeatedly measuring stabilizer syndromes and using a classical decoder to infer corrections. Modern surface-code decoders are increasingly calibration-aware: they use recent device behavior to set priors such as matching-graph edge probabilities, and these priors directly shape the selected correction. We identify the prior-update path as an overlooked integrity-critical attack surface: a poisoned prior can change decoding decisions even when the syndrome stream, logical labels, and decoder implementation are unchanged. This makes prior poisoning different from ordinary syndrome anomalies and difficult for raw syndrome-anomaly tests to detect. We introduce PriorGuard, a lightweight semantic guard that checks proposed prior changes on high-influence detector-graph entries against private syndrome-derived evidence, accepts updates only when their log-odds movement is evidence-supported, and otherwise falls back to the last evidence-supported prior. We evaluate on Stim-generated rotated surface-code memory circuits decoded with PyMatching. Prior influence is highly concentrated, with the top 10 percent of entries carrying over 60 percent of positive logical-error influence; poisoning only 6.4 percent of decoder-prior entries can raise logical error rate (LER) by 3.35x. PriorGuard recovers most attack-induced loss with a low false-positive rate and modest update-boundary overhead of about 1.7--1.8 ms and less than 0.31 MB auxiliary memory per update.

item.title: Near-Optimal Bell Nonlocality with GKP and Entangled Cat States
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Photon-number-resolving detection (PNRD) with Gaussian preprocessing and adaptive feed-forward yields near-optimal CHSH Bell inequality violations approaching the theoretical bound (Smax⁡=21+𝒞2, up to 22) in finite-energy GKP Bell states, cat-code pairs, and entangled coherent states without logical non-Clifford gates.

Grade 0.427 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Özlem Erkilicc, Aritra Das, S. Nibedita Swain, Simon Devitt, Timothy C. Ralph

Figure

Maximum CHSH parameter S versus GKP squeezing (dB). Shows adaptive PNRD and squeezed-displaced PNRD approaching the unrestricted theoretical bound while beating the classical bound of 2 and bilateral homodyne detection.

Asks

Are non-Clifford logical operations fundamentally necessary to access the Bell nonlocality of finite-energy GKP states?

Before

Homodyne detection with Gaussian operations and logical Pauli measurements yielded no CHSH violation (S≤2), requiring costly non-Clifford magic state injection.

But

Pure-state simulations truncated to finite Fock space (Ncut); numerical optimisation over continuous receiver parameters is non-convex and provides achieved lower bounds.

Tools

finite-energy GKP Bell states · photon-number-resolving detection (PNRD) · Gaussian preprocessing (squeezing/displacement) · adaptive feed-forward · Löwdin orthogonalisation

Abstract

Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are widely studied as a bosonic encoding for fault-tolerant quantum computing because small displacement errors can be identified and corrected through syndrome measurements. However, fault-tolerant operation requires substantially greater GKP squeezing than is currently available in optical platforms. It is therefore important to identify quantum-information tasks that can be realised with finite-squeezing GKP states. Here, we study Bell nonlocality in finite-energy GKP Bell states under experimentally motivated measurement constraints. Although finite-energy GKP Bell states support Bell nonlocality even at low squeezing, logical Pauli measurements alone cannot reveal it. Accessing the maximum CHSH violation supported by the state generally requires logical non-Clifford rotations. We instead show that the required non-Gaussian resource can reside in the measurement itself. Photon-number-resolving detection combined with Gaussian preprocessing and adaptive feed-forward closely approaches the maximum violation of the CHSH Bell inequality without implementing logical non-Clifford gates. item.title: Bosonic Error Correction with Fluxonium
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Realized standalone bosonic QEC in planar architecture using heavy fluxonium (T1q=451extextmus) and Archimedean spiral resonator, extending logical GKP state lifetime by factor of 1.59±0.05.

Grade 0.422 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold” · Shantanu R. Jha, Shoumik D. Chowdhury, Gabriele Rolleri, Anaida Ali, Lev-Arcady Sellem, Réouven Assouly, David Pahl, Lukas Pahl, Junyoung An, Farid Hassani, Hung-Yu Tsao, Chia-Chin Tsai, Aranya Goswami, Jeremie Boudreault, Jeffrey M. Gertler, Michael A. Gingras, Bethany M. Niedzielski, Jeffrey M. Knecht, Mollie E. Schwartz, Kyle Serniak, Jeffrey A. Grover, Baptiste Royer, Max Hays, William D. Oliver

Figure

Logical state distinguishability decay versus time along three Pauli axes for corrected and uncorrected GKP states.

Asks

Can a long-lived fluxonium control qubit and an on-chip planar resonator implement standalone bosonic quantum error correction?

Before

Bosonic QEC relied on 3D cavities controlled by fixed-frequency transmons with logical lifetimes limited by transmon T1q≈200 extmu s.

But

Demonstrated at half-flux sweet spot; storage-fluxonium dispersive coupling χ/2π≈23 kHz.

Tools

heavy fluxonium control qubit · on-chip Archimedean spiral resonator · echoed conditional displacement (ECD) control · measurement-free GKP error correction · pulsed fluxonium reset

Abstract

Bosonic quantum error correction (QEC) offers a hardware-efficient route to fault-tolerant quantum computing. To date, however, superconducting circuit implementations of bosonic codes have utilized centimeter-scale 3D microwave cavities controlled by fixed-frequency transmon qubits, with logical lifetimes limited by transmon bit-flip errors. Here, we realize bosonic QEC in a fully planar architecture by pairing a heavy fluxonium, whose 451 ±70~μs bit-flip lifetime exceeds that of any control qubit in previous demonstrations, with an on-chip Archimedean spiral resonator several orders of magnitude smaller in mode volume than prior 3D cavities. We prepare finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states and stabilize them using measurement-free error correction with rapid fluxonium reset, extending the logical lifetime by a factor of 1.59 ±0.05. These results provide the first demonstration of resonator control using a weakly coupled fluxonium and, with it, the first realization of standalone bosonic QEC in a fully planar superconducting circuit architecture.

item.title: The logical set of Gaussian states under the stabilizer subsystem decomposition
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Single-mode Gaussian states mapped into the square-lattice GKP logical subspace via stabilizer subsystem decomposition produce a convex XZ logical Bloch projection with boundary (X,Z)=(A(Vpp),A(14Vpp)), yielding an exact vacuum robustness of magic R(1)(ρLvac)=2A(1/2)≈1.160314. Squeezing cannot increase |X|+|Z| beyond this vacuum value.

Grade 0.392 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Santiago Zamora, Kaustav Chatterjee, Ulrik Lund Andersen, Thiago Lucena de Macedo Guedes, Jonatan Bohr Brask, A. de Oliveira Junior, Rafael Chaves

Figure

Z-component versus X-component of the logical Bloch vector. Shows the convex reachable XZ projection of all Gaussian inputs (left) and fixed squeezing levels r=0,0.5,1 (right), crossing the single-qubit stabilizer polytope boundary (red dashed diamond).

Asks

What logical qubit states can Gaussian bosonic states produce when mapped into the GKP logical subspace via stabilizer subsystem decomposition, and what constraints does Gaussianity place on their non-stabilizerness?

Before

Numerical investigations found the vacuum mapped state had robustness of magic 1.160 and identified a maximum robustness of 1.303 at squeezing parameter r≃0.26 (de Oliveira Junior et al. 2022).

But

Applies to single-mode Gaussian states mapped under ideal square-lattice GKP extraction with discarded syndrome.

Tools

Stabilizer subsystem decomposition (SSD) · Square-lattice GKP code · Navascués-Vértesi SDP hierarchy for prepare-and-measure scenarios · Tilted qubit witness optimization

Abstract

Universal quantum computation requires non-Gaussianity in continuous-variable systems and non-stabilizerness in discrete-variable systems. Yet, mapping a Gaussian state into the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill logical subspace can yield a logical qubit with non-stabilizer resources. To understand how the continuous-variable structure determines logical resources, we characterize the image of single-mode Gaussian states under the corresponding extraction channel, known as the stabilizer subsystem decomposition. Specifically, we derive series expressions for the logical Bloch vector and characterize the resulting reachable set, enabling an analytical treatment of the robustness of magic of the logical states. We then turn this geometric framework into a certification tool: by mapping a discrete-variable qubit witness to a continuous-variable squeezing witness, we obtain lower bounds on the squeezing of prepared states. We also show that ensembles of Gaussian states can violate both stabilizer and classical bounds. Violation of the stabilizer bound certifies the relational resource known as "set-magic," while violation of the classical bound enables the certification of cryptographic randomness at moderate squeezing.
